metaDescription: Six large 24 to 28-inch two-stage snow blowers compared, gas and battery, by engine or pack size, intake, throw and weight for big driveways.
expertTake: The EGO 28-inch is the biggest and most refined battery machine, and the PowerSmart 26-inch Briggs and Stratton is the best large gas pick for the money. The 24-inch gas models from PowerSmart, AMERISUN and BILT HARD are the value tier. Skip a large machine if your drive is under about 50 feet, because the weight and storage cost will never pay off. Check what is included in the box, especially batteries. A second set of packs is worth adding to any battery kit for a long drive.
introParagraphs: A large machine only makes sense when the area to clear is large or the snow is routinely deep. It trades a wider path, a taller intake and a longer throw for weight, a bigger footprint and a higher cost of ownership. A machine sized for a single storm a year is rarely worth the garage space.

Size is not a single number. Width sets how many passes you make, intake height sets how deep a pile you can take, and the power source sets how long you can run before refueling or recharging. Knowing which of these your drive actually needs prevents buying a machine that is bigger than the job. Reading what is in the box before ordering avoids the most common surprise.

products.name: EGO Power+ SNT2800 28-inch two-stage, tool only

specList.label: Batteries
specList.value: Not included, takes two ARC packs

products.description:
The SNT2800 is the widest battery snow blower in this group, with a 28-inch path and a 21-inch intake height. The listing claims up to 60 feet of throw and about a 32-car driveway with 8 inches of snow on two large packs, which is the figure to treat as a best case.

This listing is tool only, which means the batteries and charger are separate. That matters, because the real cost of the machine is the pair of large ARC packs it needs for Peak Power mode. If you already own two big EGO packs, it is a bargain; if not, price the kit before the tool.

Against the 24-inch XP it adds 4 inches of path and 10 feet of throw, and against gas units it removes fuel, oil and the carburetor. Storage is the cost: it is large and heavy, and packs need a warm indoor spot. Before choosing it, price two large ARC packs and a charger, because that bundle can cost more than the machine itself.
products.bestFor: Large drives where fuel-free operation matters and large packs are already owned.
pros: 28-inch path with a 21-inch intake for fewer lifts
cons: Batteries and charger are not included

products.name: PowerSmart 26-inch 208cc Briggs and Stratton two-stage
products.description:
This 26-inch gas two-stage is built around a Briggs and Stratton 950 series 208cc engine rated at 2,700 pounds per minute. It has self-propelled variable-speed drive, electric start and heated handles.

Against the 24-inch gas models it adds 2 inches of path and a bigger rated capacity, which together shave roughly one pass in twelve on a typical drive. The heated handles make long cold mornings more comfortable, which is a real feature on a machine you may run for an hour.

The engine brand matters for service, since Briggs parts are widely available. As with any gas machine, use fresh fuel with stabilizer, change oil each season and keep spare shear pins. If you are torn between this and the XP battery kit, the deciding factor is usually whether you are happy to carry fuel.
products.bestFor: Large drives needing a wide gas machine with a recognizable engine.
pros: 26-inch path with 2,700 lb per minute rating
Briggs and Stratton engine with broad parts support
cons: Heavy and large for tight garages
Gas upkeep: fuel, oil and plug

products.name: EGO Power+ 24-inch two-stage XP kit, 2 x 10Ah

specList.label: Rated coverage
specList.value: Up to 24 cars in 8 in snow

products.description:
The XP kit is the ready-to-run battery option, a 24-inch two-stage with two 10Ah packs. The listing rates it for up to a 24-car driveway in 8 inches of snow, a larger figure than the 18-car rating on the 7.5Ah kit.

The point of the XP is runtime. You are paying for bigger packs in the same chassis, which makes it the practical choice for a long drive where a standard kit would run out.

Against the 28-inch tool-only model it is a complete kit. Against gas it is quiet and starts with a button, but it asks you to manage packs in the cold. Plan a charging routine for both packs, and keep a spare outlet near where the machine lives.
products.bestFor: Long drives where a complete battery kit with big packs is wanted.

products.name: PowerSmart 24-inch 212cc two-stage, 6F/2R, electric start
products.description:
This 24-inch gas two-stage has a 212cc engine, a 21-inch intake and a steel auger. Six forward and two reverse speeds let you match travel to snow depth.

Its 21-inch intake is the tallest of the 24-inch gas models, which helps with drifts against a garage door. Against the 26-inch Briggs model it gives up 2 inches of path.

Upkeep follows the usual gas routine: oil, spark plug, shear pins and fresh fuel. If your garage door is narrow, check that the housing fits before ordering.
products.bestFor: Large suburban drives needing a mid-size gas machine.

products.name: AMERISUN 24-inch 212cc gas snow blower, 45 ft throw
products.description:
The AMERISUN is a 24-inch self-propelled gas machine with a 7 horsepower 212cc engine and electric start. The listing claims a 45-foot throw, which is the farthest of the 24-inch gas models here.

That throw helps when the bank sits far from the drive edge. Against the PowerSmart it is similar in class but a less established name, so parts and support deserve a check.

The usual gas rules apply: stabilizer, oil and shear pins. Ask whether the seller stocks belts and shear pins, since that decides how a breakdown plays out.
products.bestFor: Large drives where a long throw helps clear a far bank.

products.name: BILT HARD 24-inch 212cc two-stage, serrated augers
products.description:
The BILT HARD is a 24-inch two-stage with a 212cc OHV engine and 10-inch serrated steel augers. It has self-propelled drive with six forward and two reverse speeds, electric start and LED lighting.

The serrated augers are the feature to note, since they bite into compacted snow and ice more aggressively than smooth flights. Against the PowerSmart and AMERISUN it is another value-priced 24-inch option.

Check parts availability and warranty, as with any lesser-known brand. Keep the first season gentle and inspect the fasteners after a few hours of use.
products.bestFor: Budget-minded buyers wanting a large two-stage with serrated augers.
pros: Six forward and two reverse speeds

buyingCriteria.explanation: Gas models such as the PowerSmart 26-inch, AMERISUN and BILT HARD offer unlimited runtime with refuelling. The EGO battery machines need packs and run for a set time. For very large drives that take over an hour, gas still wins on convenience. Refuelling a gas machine takes a minute, while swapping or recharging battery packs can take an hour, which is the real divide on a marathon clear. Consider noise too, since a battery machine lets you clear at six in the morning without waking the street.

Large here means 24 to 28 inches. The EGO 28-inch saves passes on a wide drive, while a 24-inch is easier to turn and store. A useful check is to measure your garage door opening and the narrowest gate on the route; a wide housing that will not fit is a daily irritation.

The EGO 28-inch has a 21-inch intake, the PowerSmart 24-inch 21 and the EGO XP 20. Intake decides how tall a drift you can take without a second lift. Drifts against a garage door often exceed 20 inches, so a 21-inch intake means two lifts on those banks, not one. Settled drifts are denser than fresh snow, so give yourself headroom on intake.

The EGO 28-inch quotes 60 feet, the AMERISUN 45 and the EGO 24-inch 50. Longer throw means less rework when snow must clear a bank. Wind direction changes the best chute angle, so a machine with an easy crank or electronic chute earns back its cost in reduced rework. A strong throw also helps when you have to clear snow over a low fence or hedge.

Large machines take a corner of the garage. Measure your door, ramp and turning room before buying, and check that you can lift or load it. Think about where you will park it in summer as well, because a large machine takes a bay of the garage.

A Briggs and Stratton engine, as on the PowerSmart 26-inch, eases parts sourcing. Lesser-known brands such as AMERISUN and BILT HARD deserve a check on parts and warranty before you commit. Registering a warranty and keeping a spare set of shear pins in the garage costs almost nothing and saves a ruined morning.

specDecoder.meaning: EGO's mode that combines two packs for a boost.
specDecoder.watchFor: Large packs benefit most. A bigger pack also adds weight to carry.

specDecoder.meaning: The tallest pile the housing can take. Taller is better for drifts.
specDecoder.watchFor: 20 to 21 inches on these models. Settled drifts often exceed it.

specDecoder.watchFor: Common on the 24-inch gas models. Reverse gears help you back out of a pile.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared width, intake height and rated capacity across 24, 26 and 28-inch machines. Larger is only better when your drive needs it. A machine that is too large for the drive wastes both storage space and effort. We also considered the lifting and loading effort that comes with a heavy chassis.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power source
howWeEvaluated.description: We split gas and battery machines, since fuel and packs have different limits. Gas gives unlimited runtime; battery gives convenience. A big drive that takes an hour is where gas pulls ahead.

howWeEvaluated.title: Throw and drive
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at throws of 45 to 60 feet and self-propelled drives. A long throw reduces rework. We treated listing throw numbers as best-case figures. Self-propelled drive was treated as a requirement at this size.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership burden
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed fuel and oil upkeep against pack care. We also noted that lesser-known brands carry a parts risk. A well-known engine brand lowers the long-term parts risk.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to driveway
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each model to a drive size and snow depth. This is an editorial assessment, not a measured score. We recommend sizing for your worst storm, not your average.

rows: Two 10Ah packs in a ready kit

howToChoose.intro: Large machines pay back only when drive length, width and snow depth justify the weight, so match each situation to the right size.
Large machines span a wide cost range, with the battery kits at the top and the value gas models at the bottom.

cards.label: Gas
cards.text: The PowerSmart, AMERISUN and BILT HARD run until the tank is empty and refuel in a minute. They need oil, plugs and stabilizer. Gas also copes better with a very long drive in one sitting.

cards.label: Battery
cards.text: The EGO machines start with a button and make little noise but are limited by the packs and the cold. Quiet operation is a real advantage for early-morning clearing near neighbours.

howToChoose.note: Pick gas for marathon clears; pick battery for convenience on a drive that takes under an hour. A mixed household often uses a small battery tool for steps and a large gas machine for the drive.

howToChoose.intro: Established brands cost more but make repairs easier, which matters for a machine you may keep a decade.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A wide path, a tall intake and a drive that carries the weight. Over 100 feet, gas or large packs matter. Add a second set of packs if you go battery.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The EGO 28-inch and PowerSmart 26-inch are the widest, while the XP kit has the largest ready packs. The AMERISUN and BILT HARD are cheaper ways into the same size class.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your drive is long or the snow is deep. A wider path and a larger engine save time every storm. A wider path and a bigger engine also give headroom when the snow turns wet.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your drive is moderate. A 24-inch gas two-stage handles most storms. A smaller machine also costs less to store.

maintenance.why: Fresh oil flows in cold starts. Check the level after the first run. Fresh oil also keeps the engine quieter.
Stale fuel clogs the carburetor. Run the engine dry or add stabilizer before summer. A clean carburetor starts on the first pull next winter.
Cold reduces output. A warm closet is better than a garage. Never leave packs fully discharged for months.
Pins protect the gearbox. Carry spares of each in the toolbox. A stuck pin is a sign the gearbox is under strain.
Worn shoes let the housing hit the surface. Replace them in pairs so the housing sits level. Adjust them to match the surface you clear.

faq.a: A 24-inch two-stage handles most large drives. Go to 26 or 28 inches for very wide or very long drives. If the drive is under about 60 feet, a smaller machine is usually plenty. Wider machines are also harder to turn around in tight corners.

faq.q: Gas or battery for a big drive?
faq.a: Gas runs as long as you have fuel. Battery is quieter and easier but limited by packs. Many owners keep a gas unit for the worst storms and a battery unit for light ones. Consider your tolerance for pack charging before you decide.

Parts and warranty support can be thinner. Check shear pins, belts and scraper availability first. Buying from a seller with a clear return policy also helps. A seller that lists spare parts is a good sign.

It is the tallest pile the housing can take in one pass. It decides how well the machine handles drifts. A tall intake also reduces the number of times you must lift the housing. Measure the drift height at your garage door to see what you really need.
Not for flat drives. Tracks help on steep or icy slopes. Steep drives are the main case for tracks. Chains on wheels are a cheaper alternative on a modest slope.
Drain fuel or add stabilizer, store packs indoors and keep the housing dry. Clean the housing before storage to prevent rust. Lubricate the chute crank before you put it away.
